elements.name: SEDA
elements.what: Organizes a service as a network of event-driven stages connected by explicit queues, each stage with its own thread pool and admission control.
elements.problem: Thread-per-request servers degrade unpredictably under load; explicit per-stage queues give load conditioning, backpressure, and graceful overload behavior.
elements.named_in: SEDA: An Architecture for Well-Conditioned, Scalable Internet Services - Welsh, Culler & Brewer (SOSP 2001)

elements.name: Half-Sync/Half-Async (system layering)
elements.what: Layers a concurrent system into a synchronous service layer and an asynchronous event layer mediated by a queueing layer.
elements.problem: Synchronous code is simpler but async I/O is more efficient; the layering lets each part of the system use the model that suits it.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2 - Schmidt et al. (2000)
elements.borderline: Same name exists in the design realm (half-sync-half-async); POSA2 labels it an architectural pattern - cataloged in both realms per the same-name-two-realms rule.

elements.name: MapReduce
elements.what: Cluster-scale programming model and execution topology: a master partitions input across map workers whose keyed outputs are shuffled to reduce workers.
elements.problem: Distributing, parallelizing and fault-tolerating large batch computations by hand is error-prone; the fixed two-phase topology automates it.
elements.named_in: MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters - Dean & Ghemawat (OSDI 2004)

elements.name: Hardware Abstraction Layer (platform layer)
elements.what: A dedicated system layer that isolates all hardware-specific access behind a stable interface so upper layers are portable across boards and MCUs.
elements.problem: Hardware churn and multi-target products would otherwise scatter #ifdef variant handling through the whole codebase.
elements.named_in: Reusable Firmware Development - Jacob Beningo (2017)
elements.borderline: Design realm carries hardware-abstraction-layer (the interface construct); this entry is the system layer - two realms, bridged in 3b.

elements.name: Board Support Package
elements.what: Packages all board-specific initialization, drivers and configuration for one hardware target into a replaceable system unit.
elements.problem: Porting an embedded stack to a new board should replace one well-bounded package, not touch the application.
elements.named_in: Mastering Embedded Linux Programming, 3rd ed. - Chris Simmonds (2021)

elements.name: Layers
elements.what: Structures a whole system into stacked abstraction levels where each layer uses only the services of the layer(s) below.
elements.problem: Uncontrolled dependencies make systems unportable and unmodifiable; layering localizes change to one abstraction level.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1 - Buschmann et al. (1996)

elements.name: Time-Triggered Architecture
elements.what: Organizes computation and communication of a distributed real-time system around a global sparse time base with statically scheduled slots.
elements.problem: Event-triggered systems are hard to certify and to bound; a priori temporal schedules give composability, determinism and fault containment.
elements.named_in: The Time-Triggered Architecture - Kopetz & Bauer (2003)

elements.name: Time and Space Partitioning
elements.what: Platform-enforced partitions give each application a guaranteed memory space and time window on shared hardware (APEX/hypervisor enforced).
elements.problem: Consolidating mixed-criticality applications on one computer requires certifiable isolation so one partition cannot starve or corrupt another.
elements.named_in: ARINC 653 - Avionics Application Standard Software Interface

elements.name: Event-Driven Architecture
elements.what: System components announce events and react to events rather than invoking each other directly; an event infrastructure mediates all interaction.
elements.problem: Direct invocation couples announcers to consumers; implicit invocation lets components be added or replaced without touching emitters.
elements.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)

elements.name: Actor-Based Architecture
elements.what: Organizes the whole system as actors that own their state and interact only via asynchronous messages processed run-to-completion from per-actor mailboxes.
elements.problem: Shared-state concurrency does not scale in complexity; message-owned state removes locks and makes distribution and supervision natural.
elements.named_in: A Universal Modular ACTOR Formalism for Artificial Intelligence - Hewitt, Bishop & Steiger (1973)

elements.name: AUTOSAR Virtual Function Bus / RTE
elements.what: A virtual communication layer that connects AUTOSAR software components by ports independent of their ECU mapping; the generated RTE realizes it per ECU.
elements.problem: Automotive functions must be developed independent of their later distribution across ECUs and networks.
elements.named_in: AUTOSAR Classic Platform - Layered Software Architecture

elements.name: Microkernel
elements.what: A minimal core provides only fundamental services; all other functionality runs as external servers or plug-ins on top of it.
elements.problem: Systems that must be adapted to changing requirements or certified need a small trusted core with replaceable extensions.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1 - Buschmann et al. (1996)

elements.name: Bootloader (boot-stage architecture)
elements.what: A dedicated boot-stage program that initializes the platform, selects/validates an application image, and hands off execution to it.
elements.problem: Field update, image validation and bring-up need a stage that is independent of - and can replace - the application image.
elements.named_in: From Zero to main() series - Memfault (2019)

elements.name: Service-Oriented Architecture
elements.what: Structures the system as network-addressable services with contract-described interfaces discovered and composed at run time.
elements.problem: Monolithic integration cannot evolve heterogeneous applications independently; service contracts decouple providers from consumers.
elements.named_in: Service-Oriented Architecture: Concepts, Technology, and Design - Thomas Erl (2005)

elements.name: Two-Phase Commit
elements.what: A coordinator drives a prepare phase then a commit/abort phase so multiple independent participants decide a transaction outcome atomically.
elements.problem: A transaction spanning several resource managers must commit everywhere or nowhere despite failures.
elements.named_in: Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques - Gray & Reuter (1992)

elements.name: Primary-Replica Replication
elements.what: One node accepts all writes and ships its replication log to replicas that apply it, serving reads and standing by for failover.
elements.problem: Durability, read scaling and availability require copies of the data that stay consistent with a single write authority.
elements.named_in: Designing Data-Intensive Applications - Kleppmann (2017)

elements.name: Shared-Nothing Architecture
elements.what: Partitions a parallel system so each node owns its CPU, memory and disk exclusively, coordinating only via messages.
elements.problem: Shared memory and shared disk become contention bottlenecks; owning everything per node scales linearly and isolates failures.
elements.named_in: The Case for Shared Nothing - Stonebraker (1986)

elements.name: Sharding
elements.what: Splits a dataset by key across independent nodes so each shard stores and serves a subset of the data.
elements.problem: A single node cannot hold or serve the full dataset; key-based distribution scales storage and throughput.
elements.named_in: Designing Data-Intensive Applications - Kleppmann (2017)

elements.name: Relational DBMS Reference Architecture
aka: query processor / transactional storage manager decomposition
elements.what: The canonical decomposition of a DBMS into process manager, query processor (parser, rewriter, optimizer, executor), transactional storage manager, and shared utilities.
elements.problem: Database engines recur in structure; the reference decomposition names the component roles every implementation fills.
elements.named_in: Architecture of a Database System - Hellerstein, Stonebraker & Hamilton (2007)

elements.name: Five-Layer Architecture (RTDP)
elements.what: A concrete whole-system layering template for real-time embedded applications (application, UI, communication, abstract OS, abstract hardware).
elements.problem: Embedded systems need a standard portable stratification separating application concerns from OS and hardware dependencies.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Channel Architecture (RTDP)
elements.what: Organizes the system as one or more sequential data-transformation channels from sensing to actuation, replicable for capacity or safety.
elements.problem: Dataflow-dominated real-time systems need a structure that supports throughput scaling and redundancy by replicating whole channels.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Recursive Containment (RTDP)
elements.what: Decomposes the system recursively into parts that are themselves structured like systems, to any needed depth.
elements.problem: Very large systems need a uniform decomposition discipline so every level presents the same structural concepts.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Hierarchical Control (RTDP)
elements.what: Distributes control policy across a hierarchy in which upper controllers set goals/modes and lower controllers execute them locally.
elements.problem: Centralizing all control logic does not scale and mixing policy with actuation entangles concerns.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Virtual Machine (architectural style)
elements.what: Builds the system atop an abstract machine whose instruction set is interpreted, decoupling applications from the physical platform.
elements.problem: Portability and dynamic behavior require executing programs against a stable simulated machine rather than the real one.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture: Perspectives on an Emerging Discipline - Shaw & Garlan (1996)
elements.borderline: Design realm carries bytecode-virtual-machine (the in-program engine); this is the system-organization style.

elements.name: Component-Based Architecture
elements.what: Structures the whole system as replaceable components with explicit provided/required interfaces (ROOM: capsules with ports and protocols).
elements.problem: Monolithic structure prevents unit substitution, reuse and independent development of system parts.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Object-Oriented Modeling - Selic, Gullekson & Ward (1994)

elements.name: Homogeneous Redundancy
elements.what: Replicates identical channels or components so a failed unit can be masked or replaced by an identical peer.
elements.problem: Random hardware faults must not take out the function; identical copies are the cheapest redundancy against them.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Triple Modular Redundancy
elements.what: Three parallel channels compute the same function and a voter selects the majority output, masking any single-channel failure.
elements.problem: Single-fault masking without shutdown requires an odd number of channels and a vote.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Heterogeneous Redundancy
elements.what: Redundant channels are implemented differently (different designs, teams or technologies) so they do not share systematic faults.
elements.problem: Identical replicas fail identically on design faults; diversity defends against common-mode and systematic errors.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Monitor-Actuator
aka: actuation channel with independent monitoring channel
elements.what: Pairs an actuation channel with an independent monitoring channel that checks the actuation outcome and forces a safe state on divergence.
elements.problem: A single channel cannot detect its own faults; an independent monitor catches actuation errors at lower cost than full replication.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Safety Executive
elements.what: A dedicated system-wide component tracks safety-relevant conditions and coordinates shutdown, recovery and safe-state transitions across subsystems.
elements.problem: Complex safety measures scattered across subsystems become inconsistent; centralizing the safety policy makes it verifiable.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Data Bus (RTDP)
elements.what: A system-wide shared bus abstraction through which components publish and read common data instead of holding pairwise links.
elements.problem: N-squared point-to-point connections between subsystems are unmaintainable; a common backbone decouples producers from consumers.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Broker
elements.what: An intermediary component mediates all requests between distributed clients and servers, handling location, marshaling and dispatch.
elements.problem: Distributed components should not hard-code each other's location and transport; the broker decouples them.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1 - Buschmann et al. (1996)

elements.name: Client-Server
elements.what: Divides the system into servers that own resources/services and clients that request them over a connecting protocol.
elements.problem: Centralizing a shared resource behind a service role lets many independent consumers use it with controlled access.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture: Perspectives on an Emerging Discipline - Shaw & Garlan (1996)

elements.name: Distributed Hash Table
elements.what: Nodes form a self-organizing overlay in which consistent-hashing-based routing locates the node responsible for any key in O(log n) hops.
elements.problem: Decentralized lookup at scale must survive churn without any directory server.
elements.named_in: Chord: A Scalable Peer-to-peer Lookup Service for Internet Applications - Stoica et al. (2001)

elements.name: Distributed Commit Log
elements.what: A partitioned, replicated append-only log serves as the system-wide ordering and integration backbone that producers write and consumer groups replay.
elements.problem: Many consumers need the same ordered event stream with independent progress, retention and replay - queues and RPC cannot provide that.
elements.named_in: Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing - Kreps, Narkhede & Rao (NetDB 2011)

elements.name: Blockchain
elements.what: A peer-to-peer system maintains a replicated append-only ledger of Merkle-chained blocks agreed by a consensus mechanism.
elements.problem: Mutually distrusting parties need a tamper-evident shared history without a trusted central authority.
elements.named_in: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System - Nakamoto (2008)

elements.name: Message Broker
elements.what: A central intermediary receives messages from all senders and routes them to receivers, decoupling every application from every other.
elements.problem: Point-to-point integration of n applications needs n-squared links; a broker reduces it to one link per application.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Message Bus
elements.what: Applications connect to one shared bus with a common data model and command set, so any application can be added or removed without affecting the others.
elements.problem: An enterprise of cooperating applications needs a common transport and vocabulary rather than pairwise agreements.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Channel Adapter
elements.what: A component that connects an application never built for messaging to a message channel, translating between its API/data and messages.
elements.problem: Legacy and packaged applications must join a messaging system without modification.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Messaging Bridge
elements.what: A connection component that replicates messages between two separate messaging systems so their applications can interoperate.
elements.problem: Organizations run multiple messaging products; a bridge joins them without rewriting either side.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Pipes and Filters
elements.what: Structures processing as independent filters connected by pipes that carry data streams from sources to sinks.
elements.problem: Processing steps should be recombinable and independently replaceable; direct coupling between steps prevents that.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1 - Buschmann et al. (1996)

elements.name: Process Manager
elements.what: A central component maintains the state of each multi-step process instance and routes messages through the required sequence of processing steps.
elements.problem: Multi-step flows whose routing depends on intermediate results need a stateful coordinator rather than fixed pipelines.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Routing Slip
elements.what: Attaches the sequence of processing steps to the message itself; each step forwards the message to the next entry on its slip.
elements.problem: Per-message dynamic routes through system components are needed without a central coordinator.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Control Bus
elements.what: A separate messaging channel set used to configure, monitor and administer the components of a distributed messaging system.
elements.problem: Management traffic must not mix with application traffic, yet every component must be administrable remotely.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Canonical Data Model
elements.what: Defines one system-wide data format so each application translates only to/from the canonical form instead of to every peer format.
elements.problem: N applications with pairwise translators need n-squared mappings; a canonical model reduces it to n.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)
elements.borderline: Data-governance flavored, but an established EIP structural pattern with clear bridge endpoints (message-translator, normalizer).

elements.name: Guaranteed Delivery
elements.what: The messaging system persists every message at each transfer point so delivery survives crashes and disconnections.
elements.problem: Async integration is worthless if messages can vanish; persistence at every hop makes delivery a property of the infrastructure.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)
elements.borderline: A QoS guarantee of the infrastructure rather than a topology, but named and load-bearing in EIP.

elements.name: Durable Subscriber
elements.what: The messaging system saves messages published while a subscriber is disconnected and delivers them when it reconnects.
elements.problem: Pub-sub consumers must not miss events during downtime.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Datatype Channel
elements.what: Dedicates a separate channel to each data type so receivers know the type of every message from the channel it arrived on.
elements.problem: Mixed-type channels force every consumer to inspect and dispatch on message content.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: File Transfer (integration style)
elements.what: Applications integrate by producing files that other applications later consume.
elements.problem: The simplest integration needs no shared infrastructure, tolerating loose coupling at the cost of latency and no shared semantics.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Shared Database (integration style)
elements.what: Multiple applications integrate by reading and writing one common database.
elements.problem: Applications need consistent shared data now, accepting schema coupling across all participants.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Remote Procedure Invocation (integration style)
elements.what: Applications integrate by exposing procedures/methods that other applications invoke synchronously across the network.
elements.problem: Sharing behavior (not just data) between applications while keeping each one's data encapsulated.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Messaging (integration style)
elements.what: Applications integrate by exchanging discrete messages over channels asynchronously and reliably.
elements.problem: Frequent, immediate but decoupled exchange between applications needs a style that tolerates unavailability of either side.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Application Switching
elements.what: Splits the system into independent executables of which only one runs at a time, each fitting the memory budget alone.
elements.problem: Total functionality exceeds memory; sequential exclusive programs trade concurrency for footprint.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Graceful Degradation
elements.what: On fault or overload the system drops to a reduced but safe/useful service level instead of failing completely.
elements.problem: Total failure is often unacceptable; the architecture must define which functions survive and how the system steps down.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. - Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

elements.name: Dataflow Architecture
elements.what: Organizes the whole system around the availability and movement of data through transforming nodes rather than control flow.
elements.problem: Transformation-dominated systems are clearer and more parallelizable when structure follows the data path.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture: Perspectives on an Emerging Discipline - Shaw & Garlan (1996)

elements.name: Streaming Dataflow Architecture
elements.what: Structures data processing as a long-running dataflow graph over unbounded streams with windowing, watermarks and triggers.
elements.problem: Unbounded, out-of-order data cannot be handled by batch topologies; the streaming model trades off correctness, latency and cost explicitly.
elements.named_in: The Dataflow Model - Akidau et al. (2015)

elements.name: Function-as-a-Service
elements.what: Decomposes the system into stateless functions deployed individually and instantiated on demand by the platform per event.
elements.problem: Paying for and operating always-on servers is wasteful for bursty event-driven workloads.
elements.named_in: Serverless Architectures - Mike Roberts (martinfowler.com, 2016)

elements.name: Model-View-Controller
elements.what: Splits an interactive application into a model holding data/logic, views presenting it, and controllers handling input, with change propagation keeping views consistent.
elements.problem: User interfaces change far more often than domain logic; separating them lets multiple views stay consistent with one model.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1 - Buschmann et al. (1996)

elements.name: Publish-Subscribe (system topology)
elements.what: Producers publish events to an infrastructure that delivers them to all subscribers, with full space, time and synchronization decoupling between the parties.
elements.problem: System-scale one-to-many event distribution must not couple publishers to the identity, location or availability of consumers.
elements.named_in: The Many Faces of Publish/Subscribe - Eugster, Felber, Guerraoui & Kermarrec (2003)
elements.borderline: Design realm carries observer and publish-subscribe-channel (in-process forms); this is the distributed topology - same-name-two-realms.

elements.name: Self-Contained Component
elements.what: Organizes code into components each owning its directory, exposing one header interface, with dependencies pointing only toward more fundamental components.
elements.problem: Without enforced component boundaries and dependency direction, C codebases decay into cyclic tangles.
elements.named_in: Fluent C - Preschern (2022)

elements.name: Authoritative Server
elements.what: One server owns the true game/simulation state; clients send inputs and locally predict, then reconcile against authoritative snapshots.
elements.problem: Trusting clients invites cheating and divergence, but pure server authority feels laggy - prediction plus reconciliation resolves both.
elements.named_in: Latency Compensating Methods in Client/Server In-game Protocol Design and Optimization - Bernier (2001)

elements.name: Layered Game Engine Architecture
elements.what: The canonical layering of a game engine runtime: platform independence layer, core systems, resource management, rendering/physics/audio, gameplay foundations, game-specific code.
elements.problem: Game engines recur in structure; the reference layering keeps engine subsystems independent of game code and platform.
elements.named_in: Game Engine Architecture, 4th ed. - Gregory (2026)

elements.name: Thread-per-Connection Server
elements.what: The server dedicates a freshly created process or thread to each accepted connection for its lifetime.
elements.problem: Serving clients concurrently with straightforward sequential per-client code, at the cost of per-connection resource use.
elements.named_in: UNIX Network Programming, Volume 1, 3rd ed. - Stevens, Fenner & Rudoff (2003)

elements.name: Preforked / Prethreaded Server
elements.what: The server creates a pool of processes or threads at startup that take turns accepting and serving connections.
elements.problem: Per-connection fork/create cost and unbounded concurrency are avoided by amortizing workers across connections.
elements.named_in: UNIX Network Programming, Volume 1, 3rd ed. - Stevens, Fenner & Rudoff (2003)

elements.name: Kernel-Bypass Networking
elements.what: Restructures the I/O path so the application drives the NIC from user space via polled queues, bypassing the kernel network stack.
elements.problem: Kernel crossings and interrupts dominate latency/throughput at high packet rates; moving the dataplane into the application removes them.
elements.named_in: DPDK Programmer's Guide (dpdk.org)

elements.name: Multi-Pass Compiler Pipeline
elements.what: The canonical decomposition of a compiler into sequential phases (lexical analysis, parsing, semantic analysis, IR optimization, code generation) over shared intermediate representations.
elements.problem: Language translation is intractable as one step; the phase structure isolates concerns and enables retargeting front and back ends.
elements.named_in: Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools, 2nd ed. - Aho, Lam, Sethi & Ullman (2006)

elements.name: Protocol Layering
elements.what: Structures communication software as a stack of protocol layers, each providing services to the layer above and encapsulating its PDU inside the layer below.
elements.problem: Communication concerns (framing, routing, reliability, sessions) must evolve independently; strict layering with encapsulation isolates them.
elements.named_in: Computer Networks, 6th ed. - Tanenbaum, Feamster & Wetherall (2021)

elements.name: Interface Definition Language
elements.what: A language-neutral contract describing component interfaces and data types from which stubs, skeletons and serializers are generated.
elements.problem: Cross-language, cross-component boundaries need a single authoritative contract rather than per-language duplication.
elements.named_in: The Common Object Request Broker: Architecture and Specification - OMG (1991)
elements.borderline: A contract-and-toolchain construct rather than a runtime structure, but the established architecture-level boundary description mechanism.

elements.name: Front Controller
elements.what: One handler receives every request for a web application, performing common processing and dispatching to per-request commands or handlers.
elements.problem: Duplicating security, i18n and routing logic across per-page handlers is unmaintainable; centralize the request entry point.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Page Controller
elements.what: Each page or action of a web application has its own controller object handling its requests.
elements.problem: Simple sites are clearer with one input path per page than with a central dispatcher.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Template View
elements.what: Renders web pages from static markup templates with embedded markers that are filled with dynamic content.
elements.problem: Page structure should be editable as markup by non-programmers while dynamic data slots in cleanly.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Transform View
elements.what: Renders output by programmatically transforming each domain data element into its presentation form.
elements.problem: When output structure follows data structure, a transform is more testable and composable than a template.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Two Step View
elements.what: Renders pages in two stages: first a logical presentation independent of look, then a formatting stage applying the site appearance.
elements.problem: A consistent site-wide look must be changeable in one place across many page types.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Application Controller
elements.what: A centralized component owns the application's screen navigation and action flow, deciding which domain logic and view follow each input.
elements.problem: Wizard-like or state-dependent navigation duplicated across input controllers becomes inconsistent.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Transaction Script
elements.what: Organizes all domain logic as one procedure per business transaction, each handling its request from presentation to database.
elements.problem: For simple logic, straight procedures are cheaper and clearer than an object model.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Domain Model
elements.what: Organizes domain logic as an interconnected object model where each object carries the data and behavior of one domain concept.
elements.problem: Complex, rule-heavy business logic becomes unmanageable as procedures; an object model localizes each rule with its data.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Table Module
elements.what: Organizes domain logic with one class per database table, each instance handling all rows of its table.
elements.problem: A middle ground between transaction scripts and a full domain model that maps directly onto record-set infrastructure.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Service Layer
elements.what: A layer of application services defines the system's available operations, coordinating domain logic, transactions and responses per operation.
elements.problem: Multiple interface kinds (UI, API, batch) must share one authoritative boundary of application operations.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Remote Facade
elements.what: A coarse-grained facade over fine-grained objects provides the remote interface, bundling many small interactions into few large calls.
elements.problem: Fine-grained object interfaces are unusable across a network; call granularity must change at the distribution boundary.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Client Session State
elements.what: Holds session state on the client (cookies, hidden fields, URL, local storage), sent with each request.
elements.problem: Placing session state determines scalability and failure behavior; client placement keeps servers stateless.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Server Session State
elements.what: Holds session state in server memory keyed by a session identifier the client presents.
elements.problem: Fast and simple session access at the cost of server affinity and loss on failure.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Database Session State
elements.what: Holds session state as committed data in the database between requests.
elements.problem: Session survival across server failures and farms is bought with per-request persistence cost.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Bounded Context
elements.what: An explicit boundary within which one domain model applies with one ubiquitous language; integration across boundaries is explicit.
elements.problem: One unified model for a large system is impossible; explicit contexts keep each model internally consistent.
elements.named_in: Domain-Driven Design - Evans (2003)

elements.name: Context Map
elements.what: A document/model of all bounded contexts and the relationship patterns between them (partnership, customer-supplier, conformist, ACL, ...).
elements.problem: Teams need a shared, honest picture of model boundaries and translation points across the whole system.
elements.named_in: Domain-Driven Design - Evans (2003)
elements.borderline: An architecture-description artifact rather than a runtime structure; kind description per 42010-style constructs.

elements.name: Anticorruption Layer
elements.what: An isolating layer of translators/facades between two systems' models so foreign concepts never leak into the protected model.
elements.problem: Integrating with a legacy or external model would otherwise corrupt the new model's language and invariants.
elements.named_in: Domain-Driven Design - Evans (2003)

elements.name: CQRS
elements.what: Splits the system's write model (commands) from its read model (queries), letting each be structured, stored and scaled separately.
elements.problem: One model serving both updates and queries forces compromises; segregation optimizes each side and enables independent scaling.
elements.named_in: CQRS - Martin Fowler (bliki, 2011)

elements.name: Event Sourcing (architecture style)
aka: event store as system of record
elements.what: The system of record is an append-only store of domain events from which all current state, projections and integrations are derived by replay.
elements.problem: Storing only current state loses history and change intent; the event log gives audit, temporal queries, rebuildable views and integration feeds.
elements.named_in: martinfowler.com: Further Enterprise Application Architecture development - Event Sourcing (Fowler, 2005)
elements.borderline: Design realm carries event-sourcing (the persistence mechanism); this is the system-wide style - same-name-two-realms.

elements.name: Blackboard
elements.what: Independent knowledge sources cooperate by reading and incrementally improving solutions on a shared blackboard data structure under a control component.
elements.problem: Problems with no deterministic solution strategy need opportunistic combination of partial expertise.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1 - Buschmann et al. (1996)

elements.name: Presentation-Abstraction-Control
elements.what: Structures an interactive system as a hierarchy of cooperating agents, each with its own presentation, abstraction and control facets.
elements.problem: Multi-window, multi-agent interactive systems need each unit to be independently developed with mediated communication.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1 - Buschmann et al. (1996)

elements.name: Reflection (meta-level architecture)
elements.what: Splits the system into a base level doing the work and a meta level holding self-representation that can be manipulated to change base behavior at run time.
elements.problem: Systems that must change their own structure/behavior dynamically need an explicit, safe self-model.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1 - Buschmann et al. (1996)

elements.name: Domain Object (POSA4)
elements.what: Encapsulates each distinct unit of application functionality as a self-contained component behind an explicit interface, as the root partitioning move of a distributed design.
elements.problem: Distributed systems need functional partitioning into cohesive, independently deployable units before any infrastructure decisions.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4 - Buschmann, Henney & Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Shared Repository
elements.what: Components coordinate exclusively through a central data store that all of them read and update.
elements.problem: Many loosely coupled producers/consumers of common data need a stable central medium instead of pairwise links.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4 - Buschmann, Henney & Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Message Channel
elements.what: A named logical conduit of the messaging system that senders write messages to and receivers read from.
elements.problem: Applications need addressable, decoupled conduits rather than direct connections to each other.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Message Endpoint
elements.what: The component that connects an application to a messaging channel, encapsulating send/receive mechanics at the application boundary.
elements.problem: Application code should not be written against raw messaging APIs throughout; the endpoint isolates the messaging boundary.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Message Translator
elements.what: A component between messaging participants that converts message data from one format/model to another.
elements.problem: Independently designed applications exchange incompatible data formats that neither should adopt from the other.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Message Router
elements.what: A component that consumes messages from one channel and republishes them to different channels according to routing conditions.
elements.problem: Senders should not need to know which consumer must handle each message; routing knowledge is centralized.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Client Proxy (remoting)
elements.what: A local object presenting the remote component's interface inside the client process, forwarding invocations to the remoting machinery.
elements.problem: Clients should program against ordinary local interfaces while calls actually cross the network.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4 - Buschmann, Henney & Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Requestor
elements.what: Client-side middleware component that constructs and sends remote invocations on behalf of proxies, handling marshaling and result delivery.
elements.problem: Invocation construction, marshaling and transport must be reusable machinery, not per-interface code.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4 - Buschmann, Henney & Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Invoker
elements.what: Server-side middleware component that receives invocations, unmarshals them and dispatches to the target remote object's method.
elements.problem: Servers need generic machinery mapping wire requests onto object operations.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4 - Buschmann, Henney & Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Client Request Handler
elements.what: Client-side middleware component that manages network resources, sends request messages and receives replies for requestors.
elements.problem: Connection management, timeouts and transport details belong in one reusable client-side layer.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4 - Buschmann, Henney & Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Server Request Handler
elements.what: Server-side middleware component that accepts connections, receives request messages and hands them to invokers, returning replies.
elements.problem: Server transport concerns (demuxing, concurrency, buffering) need a dedicated reusable layer below dispatch.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4 - Buschmann, Henney & Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Replicated Component Group
elements.what: Deploys a component as a coordinated group of replicas presented as one logical component, for availability or load distribution.
elements.problem: A single component instance is a single point of failure and a throughput ceiling.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4 - Buschmann, Henney & Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Container (component container)
elements.what: An execution environment that hosts components and transparently provides them technical services (lifecycle, transactions, security, persistence).
elements.problem: Business components should not each implement cross-cutting technical services; the container supplies them declaratively.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4 - Buschmann, Henney & Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Activator
elements.what: Activates services or components on demand when requests arrive and may deactivate them when idle, instead of keeping them resident.
elements.problem: Keeping rarely used services permanently running wastes resources; activation trades startup latency for footprint.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4 - Buschmann, Henney & Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Authorization (security pattern)
elements.what: A system-level structure defining which subjects may perform which actions on which protected resources, enforced at guarded access points.
elements.problem: Ad hoc permission checks scattered through a system are inconsistent and unauditable; the rights structure must be explicit.
elements.named_in: Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering - Schumacher et al. (2006)

elements.name: Failover
elements.what: On failure of an active unit, service is switched to a redundant standby unit that assumes its role.
elements.problem: Continuity of service across unit failures requires a designated takeover path and role reassignment.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Redundancy
elements.what: Provisions extra units - in space, time or information - beyond the minimum needed, so faults can be detected, masked or recovered.
elements.problem: Fault tolerance is impossible without something extra to fall back on; redundancy is the architectural provisioning decision.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Units of Mitigation
elements.what: Divides the system into the units within which errors are contained and recovery is performed - the granularity of restart and repair.
elements.problem: Recovery scope must be decided architecturally: too large and everything restarts, too small and coordination explodes.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Error Containment Barrier
elements.what: Establishes structural boundaries that stop errors from propagating beyond the unit in which they occur.
elements.problem: Errors that cross component boundaries corrupt the rest of the system before detection.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Someone in Charge
elements.what: For every fault-tolerance activity some identified component is in charge of seeing it through to completion.
elements.problem: Recovery actions with no owner stall when the initiating component itself fails.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Fault Observer
elements.what: A system-wide component that collects fault reports from everywhere and publishes them to interested parties (operators, loggers, recovery agents).
elements.problem: Fault information scattered across reporters never forms a coherent picture for diagnosis and response.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: System Monitor
elements.what: A dedicated component observes the health and liveness of the rest of the system and raises faults when studied behavior stops.
elements.problem: Failed components cannot report their own death; an independent observer must detect silence.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Maintenance Interface
elements.what: A separate interface/channel dedicated to administration, diagnosis and maintenance, distinct from the application service interface.
elements.problem: Mixing management traffic with application traffic obscures both and blocks maintenance exactly when the service path is congested or broken.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Health Check API
elements.what: Each service exposes a standard endpoint reporting its health, which orchestrators, load balancers and monitors probe.
elements.problem: Infrastructure must decide routing, restart and alerting from a uniform, service-published health contract.
elements.named_in: Microservices Patterns - Chris Richardson (2018)
elements.borderline: Design realm carries heartbeat (in-process liveness); this is the service-topology contract - related but distinct.

elements.name: Process Pairs
elements.what: A primary process runs the work while a backup process on another node receives checkpoints and takes over on primary failure.
elements.problem: Single-process failure must not lose the service or its state; the pair structure keeps a warm successor.
elements.named_in: Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques - Gray & Reuter (1992)

elements.name: Saga
elements.what: Decomposes a long-lived, cross-service transaction into a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions to undo completed steps on failure.
elements.problem: Distributed ACID across services is impractical; sagas trade isolation for availability with explicit compensation.
elements.named_in: Sagas - Garcia-Molina & Salem (SIGMOD 1987)

elements.name: Model-View-Presenter
elements.what: A presenter mediates between a passive or supervised view and the model, taking over presentation logic and view updates.
elements.problem: Moving UI logic out of hard-to-test views into a presenter makes GUI behavior unit-testable.
elements.named_in: MVP: Model-View-Presenter, The Taligent Programming Model - Mike Potel (1996)

elements.name: Model-View-ViewModel
elements.what: A view model exposes view-shaped state and commands that declarative data binding connects to the view, with no view references in the view model.
elements.problem: Rich binding frameworks make hand-written view synchronization redundant; the view model gives designers and developers independent artifacts.
elements.named_in: Introduction to Model/View/ViewModel pattern for building WPF apps - John Gossman (2005)

elements.name: Presentation Model
elements.what: A self-contained class holds all view state and behavior abstractly; the view merely projects and synchronizes with it.
elements.problem: View logic must be testable and view-technology independent; the presentation model precedes and generalizes MVVM.
elements.named_in: Further Enterprise Application Architecture development (eaaDev) - Fowler (2004)

elements.name: Flux
elements.what: Application state lives in stores updated only via actions through a central dispatcher; views re-render from stores and emit new actions.
elements.problem: Two-way binding across many views makes state changes untraceable; a single direction of flow restores causality.
elements.named_in: Flux: In-Depth Overview - Facebook (2014)

elements.name: The Elm Architecture
elements.what: The whole application is a pure triad: a model of all state, an update function folding messages into new models, and a view function rendering the model.
elements.problem: UI state management needs a total, purely functional structure with a single mutation path.
elements.named_in: The Elm Architecture - Elm Guide (Czaplicki)

elements.name: Model-View-Intent
elements.what: Structures the app as a reactive cycle: intents (user input streams) feed a model function producing state streams that the view renders.
elements.problem: Expressing the whole UI as composed observable streams removes callback wiring and mutable view state.
elements.named_in: Model-View-Intent - Cycle.js documentation (Staltz)

elements.name: Islands Architecture
elements.what: Server-rendered pages contain isolated interactive islands that hydrate independently, leaving the rest static HTML.
elements.problem: Hydrating a whole page for a few interactive widgets wastes bandwidth and startup time.
elements.named_in: Islands Architecture - Jason Miller (2020)

elements.name: Sidecar
elements.what: Deploys auxiliary functionality (proxying, logging, config) as a separate process/container co-located with the main application, sharing its lifecycle.
elements.problem: Cross-cutting platform features must be attached to heterogeneous applications without modifying them.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Ambassador
elements.what: An out-of-process helper proxy co-deployed with a service handles its remote communication concerns (routing, retries, TLS, monitoring).
elements.problem: Network resilience and observability features should not be reimplemented inside every (possibly legacy) application.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Gateway Aggregation
elements.what: A gateway fans one client request out to multiple backend services and aggregates their results into a single response.
elements.problem: Chatty client-to-many-services interaction over high-latency links must be collapsed at the system edge.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Gateway Routing
elements.what: A gateway routes requests to different backend services from a single endpoint based on request attributes.
elements.problem: Clients should keep one stable address while backends split, move and re-version behind it.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Gateway Offloading
elements.what: Shared edge functionality (TLS termination, authentication, compression) is offloaded from services into the gateway.
elements.problem: Duplicating edge concerns in every service wastes effort and spreads security-critical code.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: API Gateway
elements.what: A single entry service in front of the microservice fleet that exposes client-facing APIs and mediates routing, composition and edge policies.
elements.problem: Clients cannot track and call dozens of internal services directly; the gateway is the system's stable facade.
elements.named_in: Microservices Patterns - Chris Richardson (2018)

elements.name: Backends for Frontends
elements.what: Each frontend kind (mobile, web, partner) gets its own dedicated backend service shaped to its needs instead of one general-purpose API.
elements.problem: One shared API layer becomes a contention point serving conflicting frontend requirements poorly.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Gatekeeper
elements.what: A dedicated hardened host between clients and backends validates and sanitizes all requests, holding no keys or sensitive data itself.
elements.problem: Exposing application hosts directly widens the attack surface; a minimal broker instance absorbs first contact.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Strangler Fig
elements.what: Incrementally replaces a legacy system by routing functionality through a facade to new implementations until the old system can be retired.
elements.problem: Big-bang rewrites fail; incremental substitution keeps the system running while it is replaced piece by piece.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Queue-Based Load Leveling
elements.what: A queue between a task producer and a service absorbs bursts so the service processes at its sustainable rate.
elements.problem: Direct invocation propagates load spikes into downstream failure; the queue decouples arrival rate from service rate.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Competing Consumers (system scale)
elements.what: Multiple service instances concurrently consume from one shared channel, each message going to exactly one of them.
elements.problem: Throughput and availability of message processing must scale by adding instances without coordination between them.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)
elements.borderline: Design realm carries competing-consumers (in-process form); this is the multi-instance system form - same-name-two-realms.

elements.name: Scheduler Agent Supervisor
elements.what: A scheduler drives distributed steps via agents while a supervisor tracks step state and triggers recovery or compensation for failed steps.
elements.problem: Distributed workflows need built-in observation and self-healing when individual remote actions fail.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Leader Election
elements.what: Cooperating instances elect exactly one leader to perform a coordinating role, re-electing when the leader fails.
elements.problem: Some actions must be done by exactly one instance in a fleet of identical peers, despite failures.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Deployment Stamps
elements.what: Deploys the whole system as repeated identical units (stamps), each hosting a subset of tenants/load.
elements.problem: Scaling and blast-radius control by unit replication rather than growing one shared deployment.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Geode
elements.what: Deploys the service as a set of geographically distributed active-active nodes, any of which can serve any request against replicated data.
elements.problem: Global latency and regional failure tolerance require serving every user from a nearby, fully capable node.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Federated Identity
elements.what: Authentication is delegated to an external trusted identity provider; applications consume issued tokens instead of managing credentials.
elements.problem: Per-application credential silos multiply attack surface and user friction across systems.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Valet Key
elements.what: The application issues clients a restricted token granting direct, time-limited access to a specific resource or store, bypassing the application for data transfer.
elements.problem: Proxying bulk data through the application wastes its capacity; scoped tokens grant safe direct access.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Static Content Hosting
elements.what: Static content is served from dedicated storage/CDN services instead of the application's compute instances.
elements.problem: Serving immutable assets from application servers wastes expensive compute on cacheable bytes.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: External Configuration Store
elements.what: Configuration for all application instances is moved to a central external store fetched at startup/run time.
elements.problem: Per-deployment config files diverge across instances and redeploys; centralization gives one managed source.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Sequential Convoy
elements.what: Related messages are grouped into convoys processed in order by a single consumer, while unrelated convoys proceed in parallel.
elements.problem: Per-key ordering must survive in a competing-consumers world that otherwise destroys sequence.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Asynchronous Request-Reply
elements.what: A client-facing request is accepted immediately with a status/result endpoint while backend processing completes asynchronously.
elements.problem: Long-running backend work cannot hold client connections open; the reply channel is decoupled from the request.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Choreography
elements.what: Services coordinate a workflow by reacting to each other's events, with no central controller owning the process.
elements.problem: A central orchestrator is a coupling and availability bottleneck; choreography distributes the flow logic into participants.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Compute Resource Consolidation
elements.what: Multiple tasks or operations are consolidated into shared compute units to raise utilization and cut cost.
elements.problem: One deployment unit per small task wastes allocated capacity; packing trades isolation for density.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Index Table
elements.what: Maintains separate tables keyed by frequently queried fields over a data store that lacks native secondary indexes.
elements.problem: Key-value and partitioned stores answer non-key queries only via full scans unless the application maintains its own indexes.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Materialized View
elements.what: Maintains prepopulated views of data shaped for specific queries, refreshed from the source-of-truth store.
elements.problem: Query-time joins/aggregations over write-optimized data are too slow; precomputation trades freshness and storage for read speed.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Half-Object plus Protocol (distribution structure)
elements.what: Splits one logical object into coordinated halves in two address spaces with a private protocol keeping them consistent.
elements.problem: An object needed with low latency on both sides of a distribution boundary can live wholly on neither.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4 - Buschmann, Henney & Schmidt (2007)
elements.borderline: Design realm carries half-object-plus-protocol (object-level mechanism); this is the distribution-structure reading - same-name-two-realms.

elements.name: Transactional Outbox
elements.what: Events are written to an outbox table in the same local transaction as the state change; a relay publishes them to the broker afterward.
elements.problem: Updating a database and publishing to a broker cannot be made atomic directly; the outbox restores exactly-once intent.
elements.named_in: Microservices Patterns - Chris Richardson (2018)

elements.name: HLA Federation
elements.what: Independent simulators (federates) interoperate through a Run-Time Infrastructure under a federation object model and interface specification.
elements.problem: Heterogeneous simulations must interoperate and be reused across federations without pairwise integration.
elements.named_in: IEEE 1516-2010 - High Level Architecture (HLA)

elements.name: Privilege Separation
elements.what: Splits a program into a small privileged monitor process and unprivileged worker processes that request privileged operations over a narrow channel.
elements.problem: A compromise of the bulk of the code must not yield the process's privileges; the split confines them to a minimal auditable part.
elements.named_in: Preventing Privilege Escalation - Provos, Friedl & Honeyman (2003)

elements.name: Process Sandboxing
elements.what: An OS-enforced policy boundary around a process restricts its reachable system calls, files and resources regardless of what the code does.
elements.problem: Untrusted or exploitable code must be run such that compromise yields only the sandbox's tiny authority.
elements.named_in: A Secure Environment for Untrusted Helper Applications - Goldberg, Wagner, Thomas & Brewer (USENIX 1996)

elements.name: Secure Channel
elements.what: An authenticated, encrypted communication channel between systems providing confidentiality and integrity for all traffic over it.
elements.problem: Inter-system traffic crosses untrusted networks; protection belongs in the connector, not in each message's application code.
elements.named_in: Core Security Patterns - Steel, Nagappan & Lai (2005)

elements.name: Single Sign-On
elements.what: One authentication event with a trusted authority yields tokens/tickets accepted by many independent systems.
elements.problem: Per-system logins multiply credentials and attack surface; centralizing authentication trades in a single trusted authority.
elements.named_in: Core Security Patterns - Steel, Nagappan & Lai (2005)

elements.name: Demilitarized Zone
elements.what: Externally reachable services are placed in a separate network segment between two firewall layers, isolating them from the internal network.
elements.problem: Public-facing hosts get attacked; a compromised DMZ host must not grant a path into internal systems.
elements.named_in: Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering - Schumacher et al. (2006)

elements.name: Packet Filter Firewall
elements.what: A network chokepoint filters traffic by packet-level rules (addresses, ports, protocol) between network zones.
elements.problem: Unrestricted network reachability between zones is indefensible; the filter enforces a topology-level policy.
elements.named_in: Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering - Schumacher et al. (2006)

elements.name: Proxy-Based Firewall
elements.what: A firewall that terminates connections and re-issues them via per-protocol proxies, inspecting traffic at application level.
elements.problem: Packet-level rules cannot judge application-protocol content; proxying enables semantic filtering at the boundary.
elements.named_in: Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering - Schumacher et al. (2006)

elements.name: Policy Decision Point / Policy Enforcement Point
elements.what: Access requests are intercepted by enforcement points that ask a central policy decision point, which evaluates policies against attribute sources.
elements.problem: Authorization policy duplicated inside every service is inconsistent; externalizing decisions centralizes policy management.
elements.named_in: eXtensible Access Control Markup Language (XACML) Version 3.0 - OASIS (2013)

elements.name: Intrusion Detection System
elements.what: A dedicated component observes network traffic or host activity from outside the applications and flags patterns indicating attack or misuse.
elements.problem: Applications cannot be trusted to notice their own compromise; independent observation detects it.
elements.named_in: An Intrusion-Detection Model - Denning (1987)

elements.name: Secrets Management Service
elements.what: A dedicated hardened service stores, issues, rotates and audits credentials and keys, which systems fetch at run time instead of embedding.
elements.problem: Secrets baked into code, config and images leak and cannot be rotated; centralization makes credentials governable.
elements.named_in: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series - Secrets Management Cheat Sheet

elements.name: Defense in Depth
elements.what: Arranges multiple independent security controls in layers so an attacker must defeat several unrelated mechanisms to reach an asset.
elements.problem: Any single control fails eventually; structural layering keeps one failure from being total.
elements.named_in: Building Secure Software - Viega & McGraw (2001)
elements.borderline: Principle-flavored, admitted as the structural layering of independent controls (bridge endpoint for validation, authN/Z, and isolation design elements).

elements.name: Recursive Control
elements.what: Structures a real-time control system as a recursive hierarchy in which every component pairs its functional part with a control part, uniformly at all levels.
elements.problem: Startup, shutdown, failure and mode handling pervade control systems; making control structure recursive keeps it uniform and analyzable.
elements.named_in: Pattern Languages of Program Design 3 - Selic (1997)

elements.name: Bodyguard
elements.what: Shares objects across address spaces without full RPC by attaching a guard that intercepts and validates operations on the shared object.
elements.problem: Distributed object sharing needs protection against misbehaving remote clients without heavyweight middleware.
elements.named_in: Pattern Languages of Program Design 3 - das Neves & Garrido (1997)

elements.name: Object Synchronizer
elements.what: Decouples object replicas' synchronization policy from their functionality, coordinating state updates between distributed replicas.
elements.problem: Replica consistency strategies must be swappable without rewriting the replicated objects.
elements.named_in: Pattern Languages of Program Design 4 - Silva, Pereira & Marques (2000)

elements.name: Adaptive Object Model
elements.what: Represents classes, attributes and rules as runtime data (metadata) interpreted by a generic engine, so the domain model is changed by users, not by code.
elements.problem: Businesses whose types and rules change constantly cannot afford recompile-redeploy for every change.
elements.named_in: Pattern Languages of Program Design 5 - Riehle, Tilman & Johnson (2006)

elements.name: Event Collaboration
elements.what: Components collaborate by broadcasting events about what happened rather than requesting each other to act, each maintaining its own state from the stream.
elements.problem: Request-based collaboration couples callers to responsibilities; event collaboration inverts dependencies at the cost of harder reasoning about flow.
elements.named_in: Further Enterprise Application Architecture development (eaaDev) - Fowler (2005)

elements.name: Reporting Database
elements.what: A separate database, fed from the operational store, is structured and indexed for reporting/analytics queries.
elements.problem: Analytical workloads on the operational schema degrade transactions and fit it badly; a derived store serves them.
elements.named_in: ReportingDatabase - Martin Fowler (bliki, 2004)

elements.name: Polyglot Persistence
elements.what: Different parts of a system use different datastore technologies, each chosen for the data and access pattern it serves.
elements.problem: One database technology forced onto all data shapes serves several of them badly.
elements.named_in: PolyglotPersistence - Fowler & Sadalage (bliki, 2011)

elements.name: Distributed Snapshot
elements.what: Marker/barrier messages flow through the system's channels so all nodes record a consistent global state without stopping processing.
elements.problem: A consistent cut of a running distributed computation is needed for recovery and exactly-once processing, without a global pause.
elements.named_in: Distributed Snapshots: Determining Global States of Distributed Systems - Chandy & Lamport (1985)

elements.name: Chained Processors
elements.what: Arranges multiple processors in a chain where a small always-on processor handles front-line work and wakes or feeds larger downstream processors only when needed.
elements.problem: Running the big processor continuously wastes power; delegating vigil duty to a tiny processor cuts system energy dramatically.
elements.named_in: Making Embedded Systems, 2nd ed. - White (2024)

elements.name: LMAX Architecture
aka: business logic processor with input/output disruptors
elements.what: A single-threaded in-memory business logic processor is fed and drained by ring-buffer (Disruptor) pipelines, with event sourcing for durability.
elements.problem: Extreme-throughput low-latency processing is defeated by locks and database round-trips; single-writer in-memory design removes both.
elements.named_in: The LMAX Architecture - Martin Fowler (2011)

elements.name: Supervision Tree (OTP)
elements.what: Workers are organized under a tree of supervisors whose only job is to monitor children and apply restart strategies (one-for-one, one-for-all, rest-for-one).
elements.problem: Let-it-crash fault handling needs a system-wide structure that turns individual process failures into controlled restarts.
elements.named_in: OTP Design Principles - Erlang/OTP System Documentation
elements.borderline: Design realm carries supervisor (the restart mechanism); this is the whole-system supervision topology - same-name-two-realms.

elements.name: Bulkhead (system partitioning)
elements.what: Partitions system capacity (instances, pools, zones) into isolated compartments so failure or saturation of one cannot sink the others.
elements.problem: Shared capacity turns one client's failure mode into everyone's outage; compartments bound the blast radius.
elements.named_in: Release It! - Nygard (2007)
elements.borderline: Design realm carries bulkhead (in-process resource partitioning); this is the deployment/system form - same-name-two-realms.

rejected.name: Active-object framework (run-to-completion kernel)
rejected.why: QP-style active-object frameworks are the embedded realization of actor-based architecture; recorded as aka there. The Active Object pattern itself is a design element.

rejected.name: Query optimizer / query planner
rejected.why: A component role within the DBMS reference decomposition (Hellerstein et al.), not a standalone style/pattern; the reference architecture is admitted and carries the role.

rejected.name: Layered Pattern (RTDP)
rejected.why: Same mechanism as POSA1 Layers; RTDP name recorded as aka.

rejected.name: Microkernel Architecture Pattern (RTDP)
rejected.why: Same mechanism as POSA1 Microkernel; RTDP name recorded as aka.
